New releases dominated the UK-Ireland box office top five this weekend, with Lionsgate comedy Ghosts: The Possession Of Button House rising to the top, grossing £2.4m from 642 sites, for a respectable site average of £3,827.

Simon Hynd directs, having helmed 15 episodes of the 2019-2023 BBC comedy series the film is based on. The poltergeists of Button House are faced with the unwanted arrivals of a group of teens and a protest group, leading the ghosts to discover the art of human possession. Charlotte Ritchie, Kiell Smith-Bynoe, Lolly Adefope, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby and Martha Howe-Douglas reprise their roles from the show. Including previews, it’s on £2.5m.

Warner Bros’ Clayface is in second place, opening with £1.9m this weekend from 576 locations for a site average of £3,350. Topped up with £82,000 in previews, its total is £2m. Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie star in the third film in the relaunched DC Universe franchise. James Watkins directs the story of a rising Hollywood star whose body gets turned into clay. The film has topped the weekend’s global box office chart .

Amazon MGM’s mockumentary Ali G: Who Iz I? opened to £1.3m from 458 locations, for a site average of £2,838. Despite advertising the film as a one-weekend only cinema release, the film will now remain open for UK-Ireland holdover bookings next weekend.

It is the sixth best opening for a comedy at the UK-Ireland box office this year but is down on Sasha Baron Cohen’s previous cinematic outings. The last Ali G film, Ali G Indahouse , opened to £3.2m in 2002. The Dictator and Bruno opened at around £5m in 2012 and 2009 respectively, while Borat grossed £6.2m in its opening weekend in 2006.

Morgana Robinson stars as Ali G’s pregnant girlfriend, with the titular character travelling to the US in a misguided attempt to revive his talk show and support his growing family.

Last weekend’s UK-Ireland box office number one, Paramount’s martial arts film Street Fighter , kicked up £1m in its second weekend, and is now on £4.3m overall.

Black Bear’s Wildwood grossed £983,000 in its opening weekend, which was the distributor’s widest ever release, at 655 sites. The location average for the Laika animation and BFI London Film Festival world premiere was £1,501, with a total including previews of £1m. Travis Knight, CEO of US animation studio Laika, directs.

Universal animation Forgotten Island dropped 25% in its second session for a weekend gross of £938,000 and an overall figure of £2.9m.

Amazon MGM’s Verity starring Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson added £642,000 in its fourth weekend, released via Sony, and is now on £10.8m overall.

Universal horror Other Mommy ’s third weekend stirred up £432,000, a 50% drop on its second weekend, for a total of £4.7m.

Paramount’s survival thriller Heart Of The Beast, led by Brad Pitt, grossed £281,000 in its fifth weekend, now on just shy of £7m.

Sony’s Resident Evil grossed £229,000 in its sixth weekend, for a total of £14.2m.

Sky theatrical record

In its sixth weekend on release, Shaun The Sheep: The Beast Of Mossy Bottom grossed £307,000, an increase of 16% on its previous session – likely boosted by the start of the school half-term holidays. It is now the highest-grossing theatrical Sky Original film of all time, beating previous record holder Ellen Kuras’s Lee , which brought in £4.5m in September 2024. Studiocanal handled the theatrical release on behalf of Sky.

In event cinema, Trafalgar Releasing’s BTS World Tour Arirang In Buenos Aires grossed £237,000 from 231 locations after a Sunday release, for a site average of £1,036. A mini-festival of other K-pop concert films were released the day before at 43 sites: Enhypen: World Tour (Blood Saga) grossed £11,200 (site average of £261); Tomorrow X Together World Tour ‘Act: Tomorrow’ grossed £8,100 (site average of £189); and Hybe Cheering Party grossed £3,300 (site average of £76).

Mubi started with £198,000 from 86 locations for Pawel Pawlikowski’s Cannes Competition title Fatherland , about Nobel-winning author Thomas Mann and his daughter Erika, starring Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller. The site average is £2,302, and a total opening including previews of £310,000.

In its fifth weekend, Universal’s Sense And Sensibility brought in £193,000, just a 13% drop on its previous session. Georgia Oakley’s Jane Austen adaptation is up to £6.4m overall.

Universal’s The Odyssey was up 2% on its previous session in its 15th weekend on release, grossing £176,000, with a £88m total.

Taika Waititi’s BFI London Film Festival world premiere Klara And The Sun , an adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 sci-fi novel starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams, opened to £176,000 from 368 locations for Sony. The site average was £477.

Paramount animation Tad And The Magic Lamp opened to £175,000 from 502 sites, for a venue average of £349. Its cumulative figure including £102,000 in previews is £277,000.

Dogwoof’s Gaza documentary NAZA held strong on its second weekend, adding £134,000, a drop of only 23% from opening. Its total is now £548,000.

Sony’s The Social Reckoning brought in £118,000 in its third weekend, bringing its total to £1.6m.

Kazoo Films’ animation Monster Mia, about a young girl who starts at a monster academy as the only human and directed by Verena Fels, grossed £64,000 from 342 sites, for a location average of £187. Plus previews, it’s up to £166,000.

Warner Bros’ Tom Cruise-led Digger added £62,000 in its fourth session, now on just shy of £3m overall.

Trafalgar also released Noel Coward’s comedy play Fallen Angels, grossing £96,000 mostly from Sunday, for a site average of £269 from 355 locations. Including its Thursday opening, its total is £204,000.

On its 13th session, Spider-Man: Brand New Day added £61,000 for Sony, for a £100.2m total.

In its seventh weekend on release, Studiocanal’s Pressure added £49,000, a 47% drop on its previous weekend. Its total is now £7.3m.

Moviegoers Entertainment’s Hindi-language spy comedy Udta Teer, the directorial debut of Aakash Kaushik, opened to £46,000 from 78 sites, for a location average of £588.

Paramount’s Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie added £49,000 in its 12th weekend on release, cumulating £6.5m.

Park Circus’ Scream re-release scared up £33,000 from 297 locations, for a site average of £110.

A Scottish Ballet reimagining of Romeo And Juliet titled These Violent Delights , handled by Tull Stories, grossed £6,500 overall after an event opening on Wednesday (October 21), with £204 from three sites across the weekend, averaging £68.

Mubi’s documentary Making Marie Antoinette , directed by the late Eleanor Coppola about her daughter Sofia’s directing of 2006’s Marie Antoinette, opened to £1,302 from six locations, for a venue average of £217, and an overall figure including previews of £18,000.

‘You Can See Everything’ climbs in second weekend at US box office, ‘Clayface’ rules on $24m

article_text:
Preview

13 Art Films to See at DOC NYC

Documentaries on a giant pencil that became a local watering hole, the afterlife of Frida Kahlo through her image, and collagist Romare Bearden are among the festival’s most enticing offerings.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff (all images courtesy DOC NYC)

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I'd like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets.

The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question — and more regarding documentary's capacity to sensitively portray communities currently under threat, examine artists' legacies, and narrate some of art's most idiosyncratic stories. We’ve selected 13 films we’re looking forward to seeing in-person or online at the festival's 17th edition.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away

Village East by Angelika , 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village Nov. 14 & 16

Go to any gift shop in an art museum, and there’s a decent chance you’ll find Frida Kahlo’s image draped over mugs, t-shirts, or decorative tapestries. Simultaneously a political icon, feminist celebrity, and a global household brand, Kahlo presents an interesting case study about how artists’ images define their legacy long after their deaths. Director Trisha Ziff taps into the commercial fascination with Kahlo and how her image has taken on a distinct life from her motivations and work.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs

SVA Theatre , 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea Nov. 11

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026), directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi

Èlia Gasull Balada’s and Matteo Norzi’s documentary on Indigenous artist Sara Flores (Shipibo-Konibo) was born out of a decade-long collaboration during which the painter began to receive international recognition. Using natural dyes sourced from her home in the Peruvian Amazon, Flores paints intricate geometric patterns with striking symmetry. Equally channeling the visual and matrilineal language of the Shipibo-Konibo practice of Kené, Flores creates works as a form of resistance against environmental, political, and social ills.

title_original: Strife at Tom of Finland Foundation as Cofounder Levels Accusations and the Board Claims Harassment
editorial_title_zh: Tom of Finland 基金会内讧：联合创始人提出指控，董事会称遭到骚扰
editorial_excerpt_zh: 新任董事会领导人表示，他们正努力确保遵守规范非营利组织的法律。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于这位名为 Tom of Finland 的艺术家来说，获得认可是一条漫长的路。他起步于酷儿情色地下圈，在1950年代向《Physique Pictorial》等杂志投稿，画中 gay 男性拥有令人瞠目的体格，常穿着皮革恋物装备，从事同样令人瞠目的性行为，有时这些作品被打上色情标签。", "links": [{"text": "Tom of Finland", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/tom-of-finland/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管出身如此，他已获得国际声誉。2014年芬兰邮政发行献给这位艺术家的邮票时，在发售前就有来自约178个国家的买家下单。电影人约翰·沃特斯和评论家卡米拉·帕格利亚为 Taschen 2016年出版的那本关于这位艺术家的巨著撰稿。2017年，一部以他生平为题材的音乐剧在他的祖国开演，超过60场的演出全部售罄。2023年在赫尔辛基奇亚斯玛当代艺术博物馆举办的展览大获成功；《Frieze》称他为“该国最伟大的文化输出之一”。这位艺术家由在洛杉矶和纽约设有空间的 David Kordansky 画廊以及柏林的 Galerie Judin 代理。", "links": [{"text": "Frieze", "url": "https://www.frieze.com/article/tom-of-finland-bold-journey-review-2023"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但如今，围绕 Tom of Finland 基金会的管理和方向出现了重大冲突。该基金会位于洛杉矶，致力于保存这位本名 Touko Laaksonen（1920–1991）的艺术家的遗产。据董事会称，基金会保管着这位艺术家的作品收藏，估值达数千万美元；他们表示，直到最近，这些作品一直存放在 Tom House 车道上的一个储藏单元里。Tom House 位于回声公园街区，是这位艺术家生前居住的地方，也长期是基金会总部所在地。（Rizzoli 于2016年出版了一本关于这栋房子的书。）该区域最近被重新划为野火高风险区；董事会称，此后为安全起见，这批收藏已被转移至一座博物馆级设施。", "links": [{"text": "a book", "url": "https://www.rizzolibookstore.com/product/tom-house-tom-finland-los-angeles?srsltid=AU7gw4WTf0SF9w_iS54s_B2VobNzOHeAsgXC-Ptk8l2YBknJzOoqqJNZ"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Tom-of-Finland-musical.jpg?w=400", "alt": "2017年1月25日，在图尔库市剧院，Olli Rahkonen（右起第三位）饰演 Touko Laaksonen，舞者们在音乐剧《Tom of Finland》的排练中表演。\n这部关于 gay 解放和 LGBT 权利的戏剧将于2017年1月27日首演。/ AFP / Lehtikuva / Emmi Korhonen / Finland OUT        （照片署名应为 EMMI KORHONEN/AFP via Getty Images）", "caption": "2017年1月25日，在图尔库市剧院，Olli Rahkonen（右起第三位）饰演 Touko Laaksonen，舞者们在音乐剧《Tom of Finland》的排练中表演。AFP via Getty Images", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会正面临 Durk Dehner 及其伴侣 S. R. Sharp 的指控。Dehner 于1984年与这位艺术家共同创立了基金会；Sharp 告诉 ARTnews，几十年来他在基金会断断续续地任职。他们还面临其他内部人士相当大的不满和猜疑，这些人匿名发言，或是担心遭到报复，或是为了保护未来的就业机会。Dehner 在9月19日的一则 Instagram 帖子中甚至称领导层为“流氓董事会”。他告诉 ARTnews，他确信这个大多以纽约为基地的董事会意图把该组织从洛杉矶弄走。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在给 ARTnews 的电子邮件声明中，董事会详细解释了自己的行动，并为自己的领导辩护。这个五人董事会目前由常驻纽约的主席 Robert Knox Hayes 领导，他从事银行和财富管理工作。Knox Hayes 在接受 ARTnews 电话采访时说，董事会成员遭到了骚扰。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会在声明中说：“董事会的一个重点一直是加强和保护基金会。作为该行动的一部分，2026年初聘请了合规法律顾问。我们正在尽一切努力，确保 Tom of Finland 基金会完全遵守加州与非营利组织相关的公司法。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "双方在一个问题上看法一致：基金会手头拮据。根据为2024年提交的税务表格，该组织总收入约为678,000美元，总支出约为800,000美元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "一位联合创始人在争议中离开", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dehner 于2025年1月辞去基金会主席一职。同样在那时，他被免去皮革会议及比赛 International Mr. Leather（IML）评委的职务，此前有他身穿纳粹标志服饰的照片曝光。（Them 当时报道称，Tom 画过穿制服的男人，包括纳粹服装，并称这位艺术家谴责他们的理念，但补充说：“我当然还是画了他们。他们拥有最性感的制服！”）Out 报道称，Dehner 在一条私密 Facebook 帖子中为对基金会造成的影响道歉：“我违反了自己的道德准则，也知道在一个未必喜欢我们这类人的世界里，需要更多的自觉，”据报道他这样写道。Dehner 未回应进一步置评的请求。", "links": [{"text": "Them", "url": "https://www.them.us/story/tom-of-finland-co-founder-durk-dehner-dropped-international-mr-leather-judge-nazi-regalia"}, {"text": "Out reported", "url": "https://www.out.com/news/durk-dehner-tom-of-finland-foundation-resignation"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Durk-Dehner-Tom-of-Finland.jpg?w=400", "alt": "2014年12月2日，在芬兰赫尔辛基的芬兰大厦，他在 Eurobest 创意节第二天的研讨会上发言。", "caption": "2014年12月2日，在芬兰赫尔辛基的芬兰大厦，Durk Dehner 在 Eurobest 创意节第二天的研讨会上发言。Andreas Rentz", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会在声明中解释：“40年来，Durk Dehner 担任董事会主席、带薪雇员、[以及] Tom of Finland 基金会的房东，并从基金会的商业业务中获得付款。为确保基金会资源只服务于其慈善使命，董事会审查了其利益冲突政策和流程，并遵循了加强防范自我交易和私人利益输送等风险的治理实践。基金会采取一切措施确保完全遵守联邦和加州法律。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/tom-House-Drawing-Session-jamison-rockmore.jpeg?w=400", "alt": "", "caption": "Tom House 的一场绘画活动。", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "基金会在这一领域一直非常活跃。自1993年以来，它每年举办“芬兰的汤姆艺术与文化节”（Tom of Finland Art and Culture Festival），并称其为全球最大的情色艺术博览会，在国际多个地点举办。2024年，该组织与时尚品牌Diesel合作，后者支持了一项合作项目；本月，巴黎的Regard画廊举办了一场与Pornhub合作实现的展览。同样在1993年，基金会开始举办“新兴情色艺术家大赛”（Emerging Erotic Artist Contest），此后已举办11次，最近一次是在2024年。两位前员工说，除了大量芬兰的汤姆的作品收藏外，基金会还收藏了至少3,000件酷儿艺术家的作品。", "links": [{"text": "a show", "url": "https://ocula.com/magazine/art-news/tom-of-finland-pornhub-paris-exhibition/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会说，该组织近期开展的一些项目引发了警示。前员工Richard Villani告诉ARTnews，他在Raam Art Space和Rob Gallery组织了阿姆斯特丹的展览，后者于1978年以一场芬兰的汤姆展览起步；两者都涉及曾在Tom House驻留的艺术家。Villani说，基金会领导层拒绝支持这些展览。Knox Hayes在一封电子邮件中告诉ARTnews，Villani不止一次被告知，未经董事会批准，这些项目不能推进，而且其中一位拟展出的艺术家由Villani个人代理，这引发了从基金会活动中谋取私人利益的问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会在声明中说：“基金会获悉了在阿姆斯特丹涉及几位前驻留艺术家的活动。”由于“这些活动超出了基金会批准的项目范围”，他们与法律顾问一起启动了审查。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会说：“律师发现了几项合规问题。根据联邦税法和加利福尼亚州非营利组织法，501(c)(3)组织必须完全为推进其既定的慈善宗旨而运作，其活动不得向与该组织有关联的个人提供私人利益。阿姆斯特丹的活动在这两方面都引发了担忧：它们超出了当时向美国国税局和加利福尼亚州备案的使命范围，并且涉及一名工作人员的潜在利益冲突。这些活动还缺少美国非营利组织在荷兰运营所需的注册，并涉及艺术品销售。基于此，基金会认定它不能正式批准这些项目。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "引发争议的艺术家驻留项目", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dehner和Sharp声称，董事会突然中止了Tom House的项目，包括一个艺术家驻留项目，却没有通知艺术家，其中一些人为了准备来洛杉矶已费尽周折、花费不菲。41位曾参与驻留的艺术家联名向基金会发表了一封公开信，称他们“对现任管理层缺乏透明度以及突然中断多个项目深感担忧”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些艺术家写道：“我们所有人都在芬兰的汤姆基金会的驻留经历中获得了改变人生的体验，我们希望这一艺术与社群遗产能够延续下去，并在未来继续发展。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会则表示，在Dehner作为房东于7月将基金会逐出后，基金会几乎无法在Tom House举办驻留项目或任何其他活动。在9月发布于基金会网站的一份声明中，董事会称Dehner于2025年1月辞职，并且“基金会已无法负责任地继续作为Dehner先生家中的驻留机构运作”。", "links": [{"text": "statement", "url": "https://www.tomoffinland.org/community-updates"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "领导层在电子邮件声明中说：“艺术家的遴选是在没有适当董事会监督或透明度的情况下进行的，董事会没有一份完整的入选艺术家名单或他们的联系方式。当基金会得知必须离开Tom House时，这使识别和联系受影响的驻留艺术家变得极其困难。一旦董事会能够确认受影响的艺术家，便向他们提供了预付租金、费用和不可退机票的补偿，并承诺将他们纳入未来的项目。我们还邀请前驻留艺术家帮助塑造接下来的方向，包括资助、展览支持和巡回驻留项目。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dehner、Sharp以及两名在场人士说，在6月30日的一次会议上，基金会的大部分员工在彼此面前被解雇。董事会告诉ARTnews，7月15日裁撤了四个员工职位，“以使运营与我们的资源相匹配”，并补充说运营总监和数字媒体经理继续留任，运营总监后来在8月辞职。（Sharp曾是运营总监。）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dehner和Sharp说，董事会没有为该组织筹集资金，并指出没有任何一位董事任职超过两年。董事会说，他们在董事会的时间并不能完全代表他们参与的年数，并称有一位董事会成员自2020年以来一直密切参与。他们还表示：“在过去两年半里，现任董事会为基金会筹集了数十万美元”，并补充说“即使在最近三十天里，也新落实了约75,000美元，用于支持展览、公共项目，以及基金会支持艺术家、保存和分享汤姆遗产的持续工作。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "冲突双方都表示，他们心中只有这位艺术家和这个组织的最大利益。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们太独特了，”Sharp在电话交谈中说。“汤姆的作品曾被藏在人们的床底下，他们对着它打手枪，而它如今也挂在MoMA里。”几位内部人士指出，像Tom House这样的场所在美国文化景观中独一无二，在全球范围内也确实罕见。", "links": [{"text": "it’s also in MoMA", "url": "https://www.moma.org/artists/28835-tom-of-finland-touko-laaksonen"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我和汤姆有着非常亲密的关系，他信任我去保护他的作品以及其他艺术家的作品，”德纳在电话中说。“我不能袖手旁观，任由这一切发生。我完全支持新的方向，但无视我们过去所取得的一切成就，并不明智。这是对我们所有终身会员的一记耳光，他们曾对基金会做出承诺。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "董事会主席诺克斯·海斯同样告诉ARTnews，他和董事会只是在努力做正确的事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们面对的是些爱闹事的人，”他在电话中说，“但我们铁了心要保护这个组织。”", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "It has been a long road to recognition for the artist known as Tom of Finland , who started out in the queer erotica underground, submitting his drawings of gay men with eye-popping physiques, often dressed in leather fetish gear and engaged in equally eye-popping sex acts, to magazines like Physique Pictorial in the 1950s, sometimes seeing them branded as pornographic.", "links": [{"text": "Tom of Finland", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/tom-of-finland/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite those origins, he has arrived at international renown. When Finland’s postal service released stamps devoted to the artist in 2014, buyers placed orders from some 178 countries ahead of the launch. article_text:
It has been a long road to recognition for the artist known as Tom of Finland , who started out in the queer erotica underground, submitting his drawings of gay men with eye-popping physiques, often dressed in leather fetish gear and engaged in equally eye-popping sex acts, to magazines like Physique Pictorial in the 1950s, sometimes seeing them branded as pornographic.

Despite those origins, he has arrived at international renown. When Finland’s postal service released stamps devoted to the artist in 2014, buyers placed orders from some 178 countries ahead of the launch. Filmmaker John Waters and critic Camille Paglia contributed to Taschen’s enormous 2016 book on the artist. When a musical devoted to his life opened in his home country in 2017, it sold out its run of more than 60 shows. A 2023 exhibition at the Museum of Contemporary Art Kiasma in Helsinki was a hit; Frieze called him “one of the country’s greatest cultural exports.” The artist is represented by David Kordansky Gallery, with locations in Los Angeles and New York, and Galerie Judin in Berlin.

But now there is significant conflict over the management and direction of the Tom of Finland Foundation, which is based in Los Angeles and is devoted to preserving the legacy of the artist born Touko Laaksonen (1920–1991). It looks after a collection of the artist’s work that is valued, according to the board, in the tens of millions of dollars, and which they say was until recently being kept in a storage unit in the driveway at Tom House, where the artist lived, in the Echo Park neighborhood, and where the foundation has long been headquartered. (Rizzoli published a book on the house in 2016.) The area was recently reclassified into a high-risk zone for wildfires; the board says the collection has since been relocated for its safety to a museum-caliber facility.

The board is facing accusations from Durk Dehner, who cofounded the foundation with the artist in 1984, and his partner, S. R. Sharp, who told ARTnews that he was an on-again, off-again employee at the foundation for decades. They also face considerable resentment and suspicion from other insiders, who spoke anonymously, whether for fear of retaliation or to protect future employment opportunities. Dehner, in a September 19 Instagram post, went so far as to call the leadership a “rogue board.” He is convinced, he told ARTnews , that the mostly New York–based board is intent on whisking the organization away from Los Angeles.

In emailed statements to ARTnews , the board explained its actions in detail and defended its leadership. The five-member board is currently headed by New York–based chairman Robert Knox Hayes, who works in banking and wealth management. Knox Hayes told ARTnews in a phone interview that board members have been subjected to harassment.

“A focus of the Board has been to strengthen and protect the Foundation,” the board said in its statement. “As part of that initiative, compliance counsel was engaged in early 2026. Every effort is being made to ensure that the Tom of Finland Foundation is in full compliance with California’s corporate code as it relates to nonprofits.”

Both sides do agree on one thing: the foundation is hard-up. According to tax forms filed for 2024, the organization had total revenue of about $678,000, and total expenses of about $800,000.

A Cofounder Departs Amid Controversy

Dehner resigned from his position as the foundation’s president in January 2025. Also at that time, he was removed from his position as a judge of the leather conference and competition International Mr. Leather (IML) after photos surfaced of him wearing Nazi regalia. (Tom drew men in uniform, including Nazi outfits, Them reported at the time, saying the artist decried their philosophy but added, “Of course I still drew them. They had the sexiest uniforms!”) Out reported that in a private Facebook post, Dehner apologized for the impact on the foundation: “I have violated my own code of ethics, and know that more consciousness is required in a world that does not necessarily like who we are as a people,” he reportedly wrote. Dehner did not answer requests for further comment.

The board explained in its statement, “For 40 years Durk Dehner served as President of the Board, a paid employee, [and] landlord of the Tom of Finland Foundation, and received payments from the Foundation’s commercial business. To ensure Foundation resources serve only its charitable mission, the Board reviewed its conflict of interest policy and processes, and followed governance practices that reinforce protections against risks such as self-dealing and private inurement. The Foundation takes every step to ensure it is in full compliance with Federal and California law.”

The foundation has been very active in the field. Since 1993, it has hosted the annual Tom of Finland Art and Culture Festival, which it describes as the world’s largest erotic art fair, held at various locations internationally. In 2024, the organization teamed up with the fashion brand Diesel, which supported a collaboration, and this month, Paris’s Galerie Regard hosted a show realized in partnership with Pornhub. Also in 1993, the foundation began to stage the Emerging Erotic Artist Contest, which has been organized 11 times since, most recently in 2024. Besides an extensive collection of Tom of Finland’s work, say two former staffers, the foundation also holds a collection of at least 3,000 pieces by queer artists.

Some recent projects undertaken by the organization raised red flags, say the board. Richard Villani, a former employee, told ARTnews he organized Amsterdam exhibitions at both Raam Art Space and Rob Gallery, which started in 1978 with a Tom of Finland exhibition; both involved former artists in residence at Tom House. Villani said that the foundation leadership refused to support them. Knox Hayes, in an email, told ARTnews that Villani was informed more than once that the projects could not proceed without board approval and that one of the artists to be shown is personally represented by Villani, raising the issue of private benefit from foundation activities.

“The Foundation became aware of activities in Amsterdam involving several former artists in residence,” said the board in its statement. They instigated to a review with legal counsel since “these activities were outside the Foundation’s approved programming.”

Said the board, “Counsel identified several compliance concerns. Under federal tax law and California nonprofit law, a 501(c)(3) organization must operate exclusively in furtherance of its stated charitable purpose, and its activities may not confer private benefit on individuals connected to the organization. The Amsterdam activities raised concerns on both counts: they fell outside the mission then on file with the IRS and the State of California, and they involved potential conflicts of interest on the part of a staff member. The activities also lacked the registrations required for a U.S. nonprofit to operate in the Netherlands and involved the sale of artwork. On that basis, the Foundation determined it could not formally approve the projects.”

An Artist Residency Program at Issue

Dehner and Sharp claim the board abruptly discontinued programs at Tom House, including an artist residency program, without notifying the artists, some of whom had gone to considerable trouble and expense in preparation to come to LA. A group of 41 artists who have had residencies has published an open letter to the foundation, saying they are “deeply concerned by the lack of transparency and abrupt interruption of several programs by the current administration.”

“All of us had transformative experiences at the Tom of Finland Foundation through our residencies,” write the artists, “and we want that artistic and community legacy to continue and develop into the future.”

The board, for its part, says that the foundation could hardly host a residency at Tom House, or any other activities, after Dehner, as landlord, evicted the foundation in July. In a September statement on the foundation’s website, the board of directors say that Dehner resigned in January of 2025 and that “the Foundation can no longer responsibly operate as a resident organization in Mr. Dehner’s home.”

“Artist selections had been made without appropriate Board oversight or transparency, and the Board did not have a complete list of the selected artists or their contact information,” said the leadership in the emailed statement. “When the Foundation learned it would have to leave Tom House, this made it extremely difficult to even identify and reach the artists whose residencies would be affected. Once the Board was able to identify the affected artists, they were offered reimbursement for rent paid in advance, fees, and non-refundable flights, along with a commitment to include them in future programming. We’ve also invited former residents to help shape what comes next, including grants, exhibition support and a traveling residency program.”

Dehner, Sharp and two people who were present say that much of the foundation’s staff was dismissed, in each other’s presence, in a June 30 meeting. The board tells ARTnews that four staff positions were eliminated on July 15 “to align operations with our resources,” adding that the director of operations and the digital media manager continued on, and the director of operations later resigned in August. (Sharp was the director of operations.)

Dehner and Sharp say that the board has not raised money for the organization, and point to the fact that none has served for more than two years. The board says that their time on the board doesn’t fully represent their years of involvement, and that one board member has been closely involved since 2020. They also said, “Over the last two and a half years, the current Board has raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for the Foundation,” adding that “even in the last thirty days, approximately $75,000 was recently secured to support exhibitions, public programming, and the Foundation’s ongoing work supporting artists and preserving and sharing Tom’s legacy.”

Both sides of the conflict say they have only the best interests of the artist and the organization at heart.

“We are so unique,” said Sharp in a phone conversation. “Tom’s work was hidden under people’s beds and they jacked off to it, and it’s also in MoMA .” Several insiders noted that a site like Tom House is unique in the American cultural landscape, and indeed rare on a global scale.

“I had a very close and intimate relationship with Tom, and he trusted me to protect his work and that of other artists,” Dehner said in a phone call. “I cannot stand by and allow this to take place. I’m all for new directions, but to ignore all that we’ve accomplished in the past, it’s not wise. It’s a slap in the face for all of our lifetime members who have committed to the foundation.”

Board head Knox Hayes likewise tells ARTnews he and the board are only trying to do the right thing.

“We are dealing with hell-raisers,” he said in a phone call, “but we are hell-bent on protecting this organization.”
excerpt_original: New board leaders say they are working to ensure compliance with laws governing nonprofits.

Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I’ve always been a peacenik,” says Sanders. “I got locked in a cell in 1961 for protesting against nuclear armed submarines, and today I’m protesting against the Trumpster. I don’t subscribe to apathy and nihilism.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ff905e3a1c3de881d3a81568bd4ac7ef6a6e46eb/0_0_3542_3371/master/3542.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "The Fugs in 1968. We gave him his first wah-wah pedal. Nice, talented guy”), to name just a few of his associates. In concert, the Fugs shared bills with the Velvet Underground, the Stooges and the Grateful Dead, but the biggest impression was made by a then unknown band who opened for the Fugs in Detroit’s Grande Ballroom in March 1968. “I’d never heard of Sly and the Family Stone,” Sanders recalls. “They came on and aroused the audience to ecstasy. When we came on, everyone was limp, worn out by how high Sly had taken them.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sanders and his bandmates Tuli Kupferberg and Ken Weaver were rudimentary musicians who fused street theatre and dadaist spectacle with poetry and ramshackle songs. Long-haired, anti-war, pro-drugs and articulate, the Fugs attracted plenty of media attention but never troubled the Top 40 and are relatively little known today, so Fugs Film! allows a fresh look at a band at the heart of a nascent counterculture. Blending archive footage with contemporary interviews, director Chuck Smith’s film focuses on New York when it was a cheap city to live in, and many artists shared the absurdist mentality of the west coast’s “merry prankster” dropout hippie-artists."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9fad78e5adafa8b4fab99a8de1b4be0dcafbec2e/0_0_3024_3629/master/3024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Sanders on the cover of Life magazine in 1967.", "caption": "‘I wanted to meet the best minds of my generation – and I did’ … Sanders on the cover of Life magazine in 1967. Photograph: Life Magazine", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Inspired by Ginsberg’s epic poem Howl, Sanders had hitchhiked from Kansas to New York City as a teenager. “I wanted to meet ‘the best minds of my generation’, as Allen put it – and I did,” he says. “Both Tuli and I came from the beat poetry scene. We formed the Fugs to blend poetry with rock’n’roll after seeing beat poets dancing to a jukebox playing Martha Reeves and the Vandellas and the Beatles. It seemed an obvious thing to do.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sanders’ literary leanings meant he also ran the city’s Peace Eye Bookstore and published the cheaply mimeographed zine Fuck You/A Magazine of the Arts, which featured writing by Burroughs, Norman Mailer, Ginsberg and other beat poets such as Gregory Corso."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Fuck You’s motto was ‘total assault on the culture,’” recalls Sanders. “We thought we could change the world with words. I sent copies to Picasso, Beckett, Sartre, Castro and Khrushchev inviting contributions, but none of them replied.” He laughs at his youthful audacity, adding that he did get attention from the NYPD, who attempted to prosecute Sanders for obscenity: Fuck You was frequently, cartoonishly sexual. Sanders was “fighting for free speech alongside the beats and Lenny Bruce,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The musicologist Harry Smith produced the Fugs’ eponymous 1965 debut album for the Folkways label. The band shifted to ESP-Disk, home to free jazz pioneers Albert Ayler and Sun Ra, but neither label had any commercial heft, so Sanders was overjoyed when Jerry Wexler of Atlantic Records – who had helped make Ray Charles a star and was about to do the same with Aretha Franklin and Led Zeppelin – signed the band."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet on hearing the finished masters, Atlantic dropped them. “Wexler told me the Ertegun brothers [co-founders of Atlantic] found a song called Coca Cola Douche offensive,” Sanders says. “I should have said ‘OK, we’ll leave it off’ but I got all pious about it. A mistake, as it meant we didn’t release an album in 1967, so we missed out on all the attention those Summer of Love albums got.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Given Sanders continually faced censorship, I ask him about Macklemore : shortly before we speak, the rapper was booted from Ed Sheeran’s US tour due to his onstage calls for a free Palestine. “There are always people wanting to censor you,” Sanders replies, “and when its a very rich guy who owns the stadiums and doesn’t want people to hear your opinion then, yeah, he can order such. For me, being older, it’s inspiring to see young musicians putting their shoulder to the wheel.”", "links": [{"text": "Macklemore", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/music/macklemore"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Fugs survived their spat with Atlantic, joining the roster of Frank Sinatra’s Reprise Records in 1968. Label head Mo Ostin had to play Fugs demos to Sinatra before he could sign them. “Apparently Frank said: ‘I guess you know what you’re doing.’” The label released the terrific Fugs album Tenderness Junction, which includes Exorcising the Evil Spirits from the Pentagon Oct 21, 1967, a recording made at the Fugs-led mass protest at which thousands formed a human chain around the Pentagon and chanted “Out, demons, out!”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The Fugs existed to protest against the American war machine, as much as we did to make music,” says Sanders, “and we understood that spectacle draws attention. So to suggest we were going to try and levitate the Pentagon, well, it might sound ridiculous but it gave a focus to our protest and attracted a lot of attention.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mailer, who attended the protest, wrote about it in his Pulitzer prize-winning book The Armies of the Night, and the Pentagon protests are now regarded as high points in the anti-Vietnam war movement. “We celebrated the 50th anniversary of the protest in 2017 by forming a human chain around the White House and attempting to levitate it,” says Sanders. “Again, we shouted ‘out, demons, out!’ and, again, nothing happened. Just as the Vietnam war continued for another nine years, Trump is back in the White House.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Did that make Sanders feel defeated? “No,” he replies firmly. “I’m an optimist. We must keep pushing, we can’t give in to despair. While things are terrible in the US right now, I do believe the American people will come to their senses and vote out the Republicans.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alongside public exorcisms and psychedelic hymns, Fugs albums featured a mishmash of satirical skits, choral music, protest folk, mock country, Hare Krishna chants, Yiddish songs from Kupferberg’s heritage and poems by William Blake, Matthew Arnold and Ginsberg read to music. Their eclecticism can be maddening, though the band’s first two albums are very elemental, more akin to US punk bands such as the Dead Kennedys and the Dead Milkmen in their broad humour and anti-establishment fervour than to their 60s contemporaries. Songs such as Kill for Peace remain relevant today, though I’m Gonna Kill Myself Over Your Dead Body (“if you fuck anybody but me”) leaves a nasty taste."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5ec743e4b2f78cd86ad89a5eb946ec33a7cacd07/0_0_4691_3218/master/4691.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Sanders (above “for”) and bandmate Ken Weaver protesting against the Vietnam war in 1967.", "caption": "‘We existed to protest the American war machine as much as we did to make music’ … Sanders (above ‘for’) and bandmate Ken Weaver on an anti-Vietnam war march in 1967. Today pot is legal in New York, so that’s one of the battles we fought that we actually won.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 1968, the Fugs visited Britain for the first time, where they were championed by John Peel, played the Roundhouse in London and visited Stonehenge, not returning until 2011 when Ray Davies invited them to play the Meltdown festival he curated. In between those visits, Sanders, tiring of the workload that leading a band involves, disbanded the Fugs in 1969, released two underwhelming mock-country solo albums, then focused on writing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I couldn’t believe it when I first heard of these hippies driving stolen dune buggies murdering this famous actress,” says Sanders as to why he determined to investigate Manson’s cult. “So I went to LA and attended the trials and looked at how this guy, fresh out of prison, had managed to have these teenage runaways believe he was some kind of messiah.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He reformed the band in 1984 with Kupferberg (who died in 2010 aged 86), occasionally performing and recording. article_text:
“Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence.

Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.

“I’ve always been a peacenik,” says Sanders. “I got locked in a cell in 1961 for protesting against nuclear armed submarines, and today I’m protesting against the Trumpster. I don’t subscribe to apathy and nihilism.”

Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”

Indeed, Sanders was a Zelig of the Lower East Side, friendly with Ginsberg (“A great man”), William Burroughs (“Unnerving, brilliant”), a then unknown Jimi Hendrix (“He was trading as Jimmy James. We gave him his first wah-wah pedal. Nice, talented guy”), to name just a few of his associates. In concert, the Fugs shared bills with the Velvet Underground, the Stooges and the Grateful Dead, but the biggest impression was made by a then unknown band who opened for the Fugs in Detroit’s Grande Ballroom in March 1968. “I’d never heard of Sly and the Family Stone,” Sanders recalls. “They came on and aroused the audience to ecstasy. When we came on, everyone was limp, worn out by how high Sly had taken them.”

Sanders and his bandmates Tuli Kupferberg and Ken Weaver were rudimentary musicians who fused street theatre and dadaist spectacle with poetry and ramshackle songs. Long-haired, anti-war, pro-drugs and articulate, the Fugs attracted plenty of media attention but never troubled the Top 40 and are relatively little known today, so Fugs Film! allows a fresh look at a band at the heart of a nascent counterculture. Blending archive footage with contemporary interviews, director Chuck Smith’s film focuses on New York when it was a cheap city to live in, and many artists shared the absurdist mentality of the west coast’s “merry prankster” dropout hippie-artists.

Inspired by Ginsberg’s epic poem Howl, Sanders had hitchhiked from Kansas to New York City as a teenager. “I wanted to meet ‘the best minds of my generation’, as Allen put it – and I did,” he says. “Both Tuli and I came from the beat poetry scene. We formed the Fugs to blend poetry with rock’n’roll after seeing beat poets dancing to a jukebox playing Martha Reeves and the Vandellas and the Beatles. It seemed an obvious thing to do.”

Sanders’ literary leanings meant he also ran the city’s Peace Eye Bookstore and published the cheaply mimeographed zine Fuck You/A Magazine of the Arts, which featured writing by Burroughs, Norman Mailer, Ginsberg and other beat poets such as Gregory Corso.

“Fuck You’s motto was ‘total assault on the culture,’” recalls Sanders. “We thought we could change the world with words. I sent copies to Picasso, Beckett, Sartre, Castro and Khrushchev inviting contributions, but none of them replied.” He laughs at his youthful audacity, adding that he did get attention from the NYPD, who attempted to prosecute Sanders for obscenity: Fuck You was frequently, cartoonishly sexual. Sanders was “fighting for free speech alongside the beats and Lenny Bruce,” he says.

The musicologist Harry Smith produced the Fugs’ eponymous 1965 debut album for the Folkways label. The band shifted to ESP-Disk, home to free jazz pioneers Albert Ayler and Sun Ra, but neither label had any commercial heft, so Sanders was overjoyed when Jerry Wexler of Atlantic Records – who had helped make Ray Charles a star and was about to do the same with Aretha Franklin and Led Zeppelin – signed the band.

Yet on hearing the finished masters, Atlantic dropped them. “Wexler told me the Ertegun brothers [co-founders of Atlantic] found a song called Coca Cola Douche offensive,” Sanders says. “I should have said ‘OK, we’ll leave it off’ but I got all pious about it. A mistake, as it meant we didn’t release an album in 1967, so we missed out on all the attention those Summer of Love albums got.”

Given Sanders continually faced censorship, I ask him about Macklemore : shortly before we speak, the rapper was booted from Ed Sheeran’s US tour due to his onstage calls for a free Palestine. “There are always people wanting to censor you,” Sanders replies, “and when its a very rich guy who owns the stadiums and doesn’t want people to hear your opinion then, yeah, he can order such. For me, being older, it’s inspiring to see young musicians putting their shoulder to the wheel.”

The Fugs survived their spat with Atlantic, joining the roster of Frank Sinatra’s Reprise Records in 1968. Label head Mo Ostin had to play Fugs demos to Sinatra before he could sign them. “Apparently Frank said: ‘I guess you know what you’re doing.’” The label released the terrific Fugs album Tenderness Junction, which includes Exorcising the Evil Spirits from the Pentagon Oct 21, 1967, a recording made at the Fugs-led mass protest at which thousands formed a human chain around the Pentagon and chanted “Out, demons, out!”

“The Fugs existed to protest against the American war machine, as much as we did to make music,” says Sanders, “and we understood that spectacle draws attention. So to suggest we were going to try and levitate the Pentagon, well, it might sound ridiculous but it gave a focus to our protest and attracted a lot of attention.”

Mailer, who attended the protest, wrote about it in his Pulitzer prize-winning book The Armies of the Night, and the Pentagon protests are now regarded as high points in the anti-Vietnam war movement. “We celebrated the 50th anniversary of the protest in 2017 by forming a human chain around the White House and attempting to levitate it,” says Sanders. “Again, we shouted ‘out, demons, out!’ and, again, nothing happened. Just as the Vietnam war continued for another nine years, Trump is back in the White House.”

Did that make Sanders feel defeated? “No,” he replies firmly. “I’m an optimist. We must keep pushing, we can’t give in to despair. While things are terrible in the US right now, I do believe the American people will come to their senses and vote out the Republicans.”

Alongside public exorcisms and psychedelic hymns, Fugs albums featured a mishmash of satirical skits, choral music, protest folk, mock country, Hare Krishna chants, Yiddish songs from Kupferberg’s heritage and poems by William Blake, Matthew Arnold and Ginsberg read to music. Their eclecticism can be maddening, though the band’s first two albums are very elemental, more akin to US punk bands such as the Dead Kennedys and the Dead Milkmen in their broad humour and anti-establishment fervour than to their 60s contemporaries. Songs such as Kill for Peace remain relevant today, though I’m Gonna Kill Myself Over Your Dead Body (“if you fuck anybody but me”) leaves a nasty taste.

“Some of the songs we wrote then we probably wouldn’t write now,” says Sanders, today more professorial than hippie in appearance and speech. Other songs celebrated marijuana, amphetamine and LSD: “We advocated for mellow drugs, never hard drugs. We had a guitarist who was a junkie and it messed him up. And we avoided cocaine. Today pot is legal in New York, so that’s one of the battles we fought that we actually won.”

In 1968, the Fugs visited Britain for the first time, where they were championed by John Peel, played the Roundhouse in London and visited Stonehenge, not returning until 2011 when Ray Davies invited them to play the Meltdown festival he curated. In between those visits, Sanders, tiring of the workload that leading a band involves, disbanded the Fugs in 1969, released two underwhelming mock-country solo albums, then focused on writing.

“I couldn’t believe it when I first heard of these hippies driving stolen dune buggies murdering this famous actress,” says Sanders as to why he determined to investigate Manson’s cult. “So I went to LA and attended the trials and looked at how this guy, fresh out of prison, had managed to have these teenage runaways believe he was some kind of messiah.”

He reformed the band in 1984 with Kupferberg (who died in 2010 aged 86), occasionally performing and recording. Today, Sanders, long resident in leafy Woodstock, keeps the Fugs going with younger musicians. “I still like to jump about on stage,” he says, “and working with young musicians means they all have other bands, so its not like I have to keep them busy”.

Sanders hopes Fugs Film! can inspire others to continue the noble tradition of kicking against the pricks. Fighting that American war machine, he says, “is a constant struggle. A holy struggle. A brilliant struggle. To let the human spirit struggle against the warrior caste.”

article_text:
Films and events

Dare

Let Them Be Seen

Nolitha Refilwe Mkulisi’s debut feature – a tender love letter to Tapoleng, her hometown in South Africa – offers an intimate evocation of a community in transition.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Nolitha Refilwe Mkulisi

South Africa-Germany 2026. 75min

Courtesy of Brown Flamingo Productions

Languages Xhosa, Sesotho, English With English subtitles

Introduction

Once centred around Christianity, with the church serving as a sanctuary during apartheid, Tapoleng now finds itself negotiating shifting beliefs and identities. Blending interviews, improvised performance and observational footage, Mkulisi’s generous hybrid cinematic form embraces the rich textures of everyday life, creating a collaborative space in which her subjects represent and reimagine themselves on their own terms.

Hyun Jin Cho

Content advice

Contains racist attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

I Plant My Hand in the Garden

Playing versions of themselves as the central protagonists, Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija make a daring debut: a witty, irreverent and politically astute portrait of lives shaped by the search for belonging.

Variations on a Theme

The Tiger Award winner at this year’s Rotterdam Film Festival is a gentle and enchanting portrait of an octogenarian goat herder in South Africa’s Kamiesberge.

Ba’s Book

Ashley Duong crafts a heartfelt hybrid film in response to her father’s memoir, which recounts his experiences of the Vietnam War and Iranian Revolution.

article_text:
Films and events

Cult

Rogue Trooper

Duncan Jones brings the beloved 2000 AD comic strip to life with an all-guns-blazing sci-fi animation, about a soldier in a dystopian future who is sent on an impossible mission.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Duncan Jones

With Aneurin Barnard, Matt Berry, Hayley Atwell

UK 2026. 120min

Courtesy of Liberty Films Rebellion

Language English

Access information

Monday 12 October 20:35

Descriptive subtitles

Friday 16 October 12:00

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Biochipped genetic soldiers, whose personalities can be downloaded should they fall on the battlefield, fight a futile, violent war across a chemically toxic landscape. Time is of the essence for their mission, but a raft of horrors await them. Fast and funny, Rogue Trooper is skilfully directed by Jones (Moon and Source Code), who gives this terrific British indie the feel of a Hollywood blockbuster.

Justin Johnson

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Godzilla Minus Zero

The sequel to Takashi Yamazaki’s acclaimed 2023 film is a true cinematic spectacle that’s sure to grip fans of Godzilla, as well as newcomers to the franchise.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

Bassam Tariq follows Mogul Mowgli (LFF 2020) with this gripping, inventive thriller, featuring a commanding central performance by Oscar winner Mahershala Ali.

Klara and the Sun

Oscar winner Taika Waititi’s luminous adaptation of Kazuo Ishiguro’s bestselling novel sees Jenna Ortega play an enthusiastic artificial friend desperate to find a loving home.

article_text:
Der Freundeskreis Contemporaries e.V. hat sich mit einem offenen Brief gegen eine mögliche Schließung der Kunsthalle Nürnberg gewandt

Der Verein appelliert an den Nürnberger Stadtrat und die Stadtspitze, den Fortbestand des Hauses zu sichern und vor einer Entscheidung alle Alternativen zu prüfen.

Hintergrund ist die angespannte Haushaltslage der Stadt, in der erneut über die Zukunft der Kunsthalle diskutiert wird . Bereits im Herbst 2022 hatte es eine Debatte über eine mögliche Schließung gegeben. Seitdem habe sich das Haus unter der Leitung von Direktorin Harriet Zilch, die das Amt im August 2022 übernahm, neu aufgestellt und sein Profil geschärft, heißt es nun in dem Schreiben des Vereins.

Die Unterstützer verweisen auf gestiegene Besucherzahlen der Kunsthalle: Von 2022 bis 2025 hätten sie sich mehr als verdoppelt. Auch die digitale Reichweite sei gewachsen. Der Instagram-Kanal der Institution zähle inzwischen 10.800 Follower, fünfmal so viele wie 2022. Zudem habe das Haus in den vergangenen Jahren Drittmittel in sechsstelliger Höhe von Unternehmen, Förderern und Stiftungen eingeworben.

2027 feiert die Kunsthalle ihr 60-jähriges Bestehen

Auch der Freundeskreis selbst sei gewachsen und zähle mittlerweile mehr als 200 Mitglieder. Über 20 Förderinnen und Förderer unterstützten die programmatische Arbeit. Die Kunsthalle habe sich darüber hinaus mit Ausstellungen, Kooperationen und Projekten im öffentlichen Raum stärker in der Stadtgesellschaft verankert.

Als Beispiele für das Programm nennt der Verein unter anderem die Ausstellung "One Thousand Times" von Sung Tieu aus dem Jahr 2024 über die Geschichte vietnamesischer Vertragsarbeiterinnen und Vertragsarbeiter in der DDR sowie das 2026 gemeinsam mit dem Institut für moderne Kunst und dem Kunstverein Nürnberg realisierte Projekt "ibid." mit 30 internationalen Positionen zeitgenössischer Malerei.

Eine Schließung wäre nach Ansicht der Unterzeichner nicht nur ein Verlust für die kulturelle Vielfalt Nürnbergs, sondern auch für den gesellschaftlichen Diskurs. Die Kunsthalle sei ein wichtiger Ort für internationale Gegenwartskunst und die Auseinandersetzung mit gesellschaftspolitischen Fragen. 2027 feiert die Institution ihr 60-jähriges Bestehen.

Der Freundeskreis fordert den Stadtrat ausdrücklich auf, keinen Schließungsbeschluss zu fassen, bevor realistische Alternativen geprüft und öffentlich diskutiert worden seien.

article_text:
ファッションフォトグラフィーを中心に活躍する松原博子による「LIQUID / LUSTER EXHIBITION」が11月6日〜8日、A4ギャラリーで開催される。

本展は、ガラス作家・山野アンダーソン陽子が制作するガラスを写した冬の写真集『Liquid』（B5変形） と、夏のZINE『Luster』（A3変形）を起点とした展示だ。冬の空気と、発光する夏の空気、異なる光のなかで見つめられたガラスと風景が、ひとつの空間に並ぶ。

山野の「ガラスは液体。閉じている世界のなかで、冷たい空気とガラスは似ている」という言葉が、冬のスウェーデンへと松原を向かわせた。そうして山野が自宅からアトリエへと通う日常の風景と、そこで制作されるガラスを撮影した。松原は“ガラスに感情があるのなら、それを写したい”と考え、ガラスのかたちそのものをとらえる方法を探っていく。同じ透明な存在でありながら、異なる時間を持つ氷とガラス。氷は溶けて消えるが、ガラスは壊れるまでそのかたちを留める。凍らせること。からだに密着させること。それらは、固体としての輪郭をほどき、ガラスの感情を表そうとする試みだった。写真に写る手は、山野自身のもので、人間のかたちを扱った『mono』から続く関心が、ここではガラスとそれを取り巻くものに向けられている。

今回の写真展では、図鑑のようにガラスを見せていた写真集『Liquid』と、夏に再び訪れたスウェーデンでガラスを写したZINE『Luster』に収められた作品の一部を展示。アナログプリントによって印画紙に焼き付けられた写真は、スケールを拡張し、ミクロなものをマクロにすることで、これまで見えていなかったものが浮かび上がらせる。氷やガラスの表情に目を向けるとき、感情が現れてくるのかもしれない。透明なガラス、からだ、そして風景。松原が質感としてフィルムに収めた、それらの流動する線が、硬質な空間構成の中で重なり合う3日間となる。

Shows

Up Close: Firenze Lai Paints the Gravity of Hope

FIRENZE LAI ,

Moonbow , 2024, oil on canvas, 145 x 116 cm. Courtesy the artist and White Cube.

Firenze Lai North and True North White Cube Mason’s Yard London Oct 13 – Nov 14, 2026

Some painters give pain a color; Firenze Lai draws out its pallor. In Moonbow (2024), the yellow figure glows softly, its depleted hue suggesting sickness as much as sanctity. It stoops, one arm braced against the ground, the other pawing at an indeterminate opening overhead. With the slightest stroke, Lai registers the head’s agonizing backward tilt: the effort of looking up while the body bears down. Below, a red vein runs through a finger of the distended supporting hand. Thinly brushed, the hues chafe against one another, violent in their quiet dissonance.

The painting belongs to “North and True North,” Lai’s solo exhibition at White Cube Mason’s Yard. Where the Hong Kong-born painter’s earlier protagonists already bend and buckle against the spaces they inhabit, here flesh takes on sculptural density, each contortion calcifying under the strain of sustaining it. Color offers moments of levity: lush in some passages, desultory in others. Alone or heaped together, the bodies teeter between ungainliness and grace, their heft and mass insisting that poise is but burden, carried well.

FIRENZE LAI , Trinity , 2025, oil on canvas, 160 x 125 cm (left) and Grey Matter , 2026, oil on canvas, 125 x 100 cm (right). Courtesy the artist and White Cube.

Increasingly, Lai’s subjects grow intimate with the thresholds that confine them. In Trinity (2025), three figures interlock in a vertical balancing act against a sumptuous magenta horizon. The top form’s arched buttocks graze the upper edge of the canvas; at the bottom, swollen feet sink into a murky pool of light. Three heads bow in the same direction, in deference, even reverence, to their predicament: between floor and ceiling, birth and death, they hold each other up and weigh one another down. In Grey Matter (2026), a solitary torso curls inward, its hunched back etching an exquisite curvature against the world beyond. That world, whether courtyard or interior, is less hostile than indifferent, yet against its pressures the individual draws in its borders, folding into itself.

FIRENZE LAI ’s

Moonbow , 2024, oil on canvas, 145 x 116 cm (left) at “Firenze Lai: North and True North,” White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, 2026. Photo by Eva Herzog. Courtesy the artist and White Cube.

Moonbow traces an opposite arc. From the ground, the upper limb unfurls a tenuous curve skyward, then gropes outward, searching. The hand is perhaps stuck, but still it reaches. We follow the arm up, then return to the hand below; looking becomes a circuit between that which is sought and the cost of that seeking. A moonbow is a lunar rainbow, a ghostly spectrum cast by the moon, rather than the sun, through rain or mist. Its colors too faint to discern, it offers light without the coming of day, a dawn that never breaks. Lai’s figure stretches toward that withheld promise, feeling for a passage. When beauty shows us a direction but not the way through, hope becomes the heaviest load. What—and how—are we holding up?

Michele Chan is managing editor at ArtAsiaPacific.
